deleted.title: Recover Deleted Files From an External Hard Drive
deleted.metaDescription: Deleted files from a USB external hard drive are often still there until overwritten. Stop using it and recover with free tools like PhotoRec and TestDisk.
deleted.summary: Deleting a file usually just marks its space as free, so the data stays until new files overwrite it. Check the Recycle Bin or Trash first, since many computers keep one on external hard drives too. If the files are not there, recovery tools are your main option.
deleted.riskNote: If the drive is healthy, recovery only reads data, as long as you save results to a different drive.
stopFirst: Stop copying, saving or editing files on this drive now. New data can overwrite your deleted files.
Do not install recovery software onto the affected drive. Install it on your computer's own drive.
Do not save recovered files back to the same drive. Pick a different drive.

steps.title: Unplug or stop writing to the drive
steps.detail: Safely eject it and keep it idle until you are ready to scan. If it is a portable SSD rather than a spinning drive, read the SSD guide too, because SSDs often erase deleted data quickly.

steps.title: Check for backups
steps.detail: Look in cloud backups, File History, Time Machine, or another copy. Also open the Recycle Bin or Trash, because files deleted from an external hard drive often land there first.

steps.title: Prepare a destination
steps.detail: Use your computer's internal drive or another drive with enough free space as the place to save recovered files.

steps.title: Connect the external drive directly
steps.detail: Plug it straight into a USB port on your computer, not through a hub. Leave it in its enclosure. You do not need to take it out.

steps.title: Run TestDisk for folders and names
steps.detail: TestDisk can list recently deleted files with original names on some file systems. Copy what you find to the destination drive.

steps.title: Use PhotoRec for the rest
steps.detail: PhotoRec scans for file types such as photos, videos and documents and saves them to your destination. Names are usually lost.

steps.title: Verify the results
steps.detail: Open a sample of recovered files to check they work before you wipe or reuse the drive.

deleted.callPro: If the drive starts clicking, disconnecting, or the files are irreplaceable and scans find nothing, stop and ask a professional.

faq.q: Are deleted files on an external drive in the Recycle Bin?
faq.a: Often yes. Windows and macOS usually keep a Recycle Bin or Trash on external hard drives, so check there first. If they are not there, stop writing to the drive and use recovery software.

faq.q: Do I need to take the drive out of its case?
faq.a: No, scan it while it is still in its case. Many portables have USB built onto the drive or encrypt data through the case's board, so removing it can make data unreadable.

faq.q: Why are recovered file names missing?
faq.a: PhotoRec finds files by content, not by their table entry, so names and folders are often lost. TestDisk can sometimes keep them.

formatted.title: Recover Files From a Formatted External Drive
formatted.metaDescription: Formatted your external hard drive? Quick format is often recoverable, full format on Windows is not. Learn which tools to use and what to avoid.
formatted.summary: A quick format erases the drive's table of contents but usually leaves your data in place, so recovery is often possible. A full format on Windows Vista and later writes zeros, and that data is gone for good.
formatted.riskNote: Scanning only reads the drive, but saving anything new onto it can overwrite what is left.
stopFirst: Do not copy any new files onto the formatted drive. New data overwrites what you want back.
Do not format it again, even to a different file system.
Do not install recovery software onto the formatted drive.

steps.title: Figure out the format type
steps.detail: A quick format takes seconds to minutes. A full format takes hours. On Windows Vista and later, a full format writes zeros, so the old files cannot be recovered.

steps.title: Stop using the drive
steps.detail: Safely eject it and leave it alone. Do not set it up again with a new backup or file copy.

steps.title: Connect it directly
steps.detail: Plug it into a USB port on your computer, leaving it in its enclosure. Prepare a separate drive with enough free space for the results.

steps.title: Run TestDisk
steps.detail: TestDisk can search for the lost partition and may restore your folders with their original names, especially after a quick format.

steps.title: Use PhotoRec if TestDisk cannot help
steps.detail: PhotoRec carves files out by type and saves them to your other drive. Expect generic names that you sort afterwards.

steps.title: Check your files
steps.detail: Open a few of each type. If many are blank or damaged, the drive may have been fully formatted or overwritten, or it is an SSD that erased the freed space (see the SSD guide).

formatted.callPro: If the drive drops out, makes noises, or the data is critical and software scans come up empty, stop and consult a professional.

faq.q: Can I recover data after a full format?
faq.a: On Windows Vista and later, no. A full format writes zeros over the drive. A quick format is often recoverable.

faq.q: Did reformatting for a Mac or PC erase my files?
faq.a: Reformatting to another file system is a format, so the old data is just hidden if it was a quick format. Stop using the drive and scan it right away.

faq.q: Will I keep my folders?
faq.a: Sometimes with TestDisk. With PhotoRec, files usually come back sorted by type with generic names.

not-detected.title: External Hard Drive Not Showing Up or Detected
not-detected.metaDescription: External hard drive not showing up or recognized? Check cable, port and power first, then learn about enclosure faults, soldered USB ports and encryption.
not-detected.summary: An external drive has a hard drive inside plus a small bridge board that turns USB into the drive's own connection. The fault could be the cable, the port, the bridge board, or the drive itself. Start with cheap, safe checks.
not-detected.riskNote: Cable and software checks are safe, but taking the drive out of its case can lock encrypted data or damage it.
stopFirst: Do not format or initialize the drive if the computer offers to. That can erase the data.
Do not keep plugging and unplugging if you hear clicking or the drive feels hot. That adds wear.
Do not open the drive's case yet. Many portable drives are encrypted or have USB soldered to the drive, so removing it can make data unreadable.

steps.title: Try another cable and port
steps.detail: USB cables fail a lot. Use a different cable and a different port directly on the computer, not through a hub. For desktop drives, check the power adapter.

steps.title: Try a second computer
steps.detail: If it works elsewhere, the problem is your computer, drivers or port. If it fails everywhere, the drive or its bridge board is the likely cause.

steps.title: Check Disk Management or Disk Utility
steps.detail: The drive may be listed but have no letter, or show as Raw, Unallocated or Not Initialized. Do not format or initialize it; use TestDisk instead, ideally on an image.

steps.title: Listen and feel
steps.detail: A spinning drive hums softly. Clicking, grinding or silence points to a drive fault, so read the clicking or no-power guide instead.

steps.title: Understand the enclosure
steps.detail: If the drive is detected by USB but no storage shows up, the bridge board may have failed. Do not assume the drive inside is bad.

steps.title: Know the risk of opening the case
steps.detail: Many WD portables, and some other brands, have the USB port built right onto the drive's board, so there is no standard SATA port. Many WD My Passport and My Book drives also encrypt data through the case's bridge board, so a different adapter can show unreadable data.

steps.title: If it is readable, image it
steps.detail: If the drive appears but has errors, check SMART with CrystalDiskInfo or smartmontools, then image it with ddrescue before using TestDisk or PhotoRec. Type the failing drive first and the destination second; swapping them erases your data.

not-detected.callPro: If it is not detected on any computer with a good cable, or it is a soldered or encrypted portable model with important data, stop and consider a professional.

faq.q: Can I just take the drive out and plug it into my computer?
faq.a: Sometimes, but not always. Some portables have no standard SATA port, and some encrypt data using the original enclosure's board, so the data may look blank outside it.

faq.q: How do I tell a bad enclosure from a bad drive?
faq.a: If the drive spins and sounds normal but no disk appears on any computer, the bridge board may be bad. Clicking, grinding or silence points to the drive itself.

faq.q: Should I format it when Windows asks?
faq.a: No. Formatting can erase the data you want to save. Use TestDisk first.

clicking.title: External Hard Drive Clicking, Grinding or Beeping
clicking.metaDescription: External hard drive clicking, grinding or beeping? It is likely mechanical failure. Learn what not to do, why not to open it, and when to get help.
clicking.summary: Clicking, grinding or beeping from the drive inside usually means the read/write heads or motor are failing. Each time you power it on, the damage can grow, and portable drives are easily hurt by drops.
clicking.riskNote: Mechanical faults worsen with every power-up, and real repairs need a cleanroom.
stopFirst: Unplug it and leave it off. Do not keep trying, because each power-up can scratch the platters.
Do not use the freezer trick, tap it, or shake it. These are myths that can do harm.
Never open the drive itself. Dust ruins the platters, and it needs a cleanroom.
Do not run recovery scans, CHKDSK or other repair tools on it. Heavy reading stresses a failing drive; imaging (below) is the only DIY step worth trying.

steps.title: Unplug it now
steps.detail: Disconnect the drive. Note what you heard: clicking, grinding, beeping, or nothing.

steps.title: Judge how much the data matters
steps.detail: If the files are irreplaceable, the safest choice is a professional with a cleanroom. If you accept the risk, continue carefully.

steps.title: Be careful about the enclosure
steps.detail: Do not remove the drive from its case. Many WD portables, and some other brands, have USB built onto the drive, and many WD drives encrypt data through the case's board. Removing it can make data unreadable even if the drive is fine.

steps.title: Try one careful connection with good power
steps.detail: Use one good cable plus the drive's own power adapter or Y-cable if it has one, since weak USB power can cause clicking. If it spins and appears, image it right away with HDDSuperClone (Linux) or ddrescue onto a different healthy drive.

steps.title: Get the copy direction right
steps.detail: In ddrescue or HDDSuperClone, the clicking drive is the source and the healthy drive is the destination. Swapping them erases your data, so check twice before you start.

steps.title: Recover from the image
steps.detail: Run TestDisk or PhotoRec on the image, not on the original drive.

steps.title: Stop at the first relapse
steps.detail: If the clicking returns or it vanishes, power off. More attempts reduce what a professional can save.

clicking.callPro: If it clicks, grinds, beeps or will not spin and the data matters, stop and have a professional with a cleanroom look at it.

faq.q: Is clicking caused by the USB enclosure?
faq.a: Usually no. The sound comes from the drive's moving parts. A weak power supply can trigger it on some portables, so trying a better power source once is reasonable.

faq.q: Can I put it in the freezer?
faq.a: No. It is a myth that can cause condensation damage. Experts advise against it.

faq.q: Can I swap it into another enclosure?
faq.a: It will not fix a mechanical fault, and some drives have soldered USB or encryption tied to the original board. Avoid it unless you know the model.

no-power.title: External Hard Drive Not Spinning or Won't Power On
no-power.metaDescription: External hard drive dead, no lights, not spinning, or smells burnt? Check the cable and power, learn about bridge board faults, and know when to stop.
no-power.summary: If an external drive has no lights or sound, the cause may be a bad cable, a dead power adapter, a failed bridge board, or a failed drive. A burnt smell suggests an electrical fault, so stop trying.
no-power.riskNote: Cable and adapter checks are safe, but repeated attempts on a drive with an electrical or motor fault can make things worse.
stopFirst: Unplug it if you smell burning or see scorch marks. Do not power it up again.
Do not keep power-cycling it hoping it starts.
Do not use the freezer trick, and never open the drive. It needs a cleanroom.
Do not use a power adapter that does not match the one it came with. The wrong voltage can burn the board.

steps.title: Look and smell for damage
steps.detail: Check the USB port on the drive for bent or loose pins, and sniff for a burnt smell. Loose or broken ports are common on portables.

steps.title: Check the power source
steps.detail: Try one other USB cable and port, then one other computer. For desktop drives, check that the wall adapter is the original one and the outlet works.

steps.title: Look for lights and listen
steps.detail: Note whether the LED turns on and whether you hear a faint spin-up. Lights but no spin suggest a drive or motor fault. No lights suggest cable, power or bridge board trouble.

steps.title: Understand what might be inside
steps.detail: A bridge board fault can leave a healthy drive inside. But many portables have the USB connector soldered on, and many WD drives encrypt data tied to the bridge board, so swapping parts is risky.

steps.title: Avoid DIY surgery on soldered or encrypted models
steps.detail: Do not pry the drive out unless you know it has a normal SATA connector and is not hardware encrypted. Prying can break clips and cause damage.

steps.title: If it spins and appears, image it
steps.detail: Copy it to another drive with ddrescue, then run TestDisk or PhotoRec on the image. Type the failing drive first and the destination second; swapping them erases your data.

steps.title: Stop if it stays dead
steps.detail: If nothing works after a good cable and power source, it needs hardware repair by a professional.

no-power.callPro: If there are no lights or spin after good cable and power checks, or there is a burnt smell, stop and use a professional.

faq.q: No lights at all. Is the drive dead?
faq.a: Not necessarily. A broken cable, adapter, USB port or bridge board can look the same. Try other cables and computers before giving up.

faq.q: Can I take the drive out and connect it directly?
faq.a: Only if it has a standard SATA connector and is not encrypted by the enclosure. Many portables do not, so check the model first.

faq.q: Is a loose USB port fixable?
faq.a: It can be, but soldering needs skill, and a poor repair can damage the board. Ask an expert for valuable data.

liquid-fire.title: Water, Liquid or Fire Damaged External Drive
liquid-fire.metaDescription: External hard drive got wet, flooded or burned? Do not power it on, do not use rice or heat. Here is what to do and why a professional is the safe choice.
liquid-fire.summary: Liquid can short the bridge board and drive board, and corrosion starts quickly. Fire and heat can warp parts. Powering it on can destroy what is left, so keep it off and get professional help.
liquid-fire.riskNote: Power, heat, or opening the case can turn recoverable damage into permanent loss.
stopFirst: Do not plug it in or power it on, not even once to test.
Do not dry it with a hair dryer, oven or heater, and do not put it in rice. Heat can warp parts, and rice adds dust without drying the inside.
Do not open the drive or try to clean the platters.
Do not shake it or rinse it to remove dirt or salt.

steps.title: Unplug and leave it off
steps.detail: Remove the cable and power adapter, and do not plug a wet adapter into the wall, because that is a shock risk. Powering a wet drive can short the board and scratch the disk.

steps.title: Note what happened
steps.detail: Write down if it was clean water, salt water, a sugary drink, flood mud, smoke or flames. Salt and mud corrode fast.

steps.title: Do not take the drive out of the case yourself
steps.detail: Prying it open can break parts, and many portables have soldered USB or encryption tied to the enclosure board, which makes data unreadable if separated.

steps.title: Pack it carefully
steps.detail: Wrap it in a soft cloth and put it in a padded box. If it came from a flood and is muddy or salty, keep it damp in a sealed bag rather than letting it dry.

steps.title: Contact a professional soon
steps.detail: Corrosion spreads with time, so do not wait. Choose a lab that uses a cleanroom and ask how it handles your drive before paying.

liquid-fire.callPro: Liquid, smoke or fire damage should go to a professional with a cleanroom before anyone powers the drive on.

faq.q: Can rice dry out a wet external drive?
faq.a: No. Rice does not remove moisture well and can add dust. Keep the drive off and get professional help.

faq.q: It only got a splash. Can I try it once it dries?
faq.a: It is a gamble. Residue can short the board and a power-up can scratch the disk, so use a professional for important data.

faq.q: Will the enclosure protect the drive?
faq.a: Not against liquid. Most enclosures are not sealed, and water can reach the board and drive.

corrupted.title: Fix a Corrupted or Unreadable External Hard Drive
corrupted.metaDescription: External hard drive shows RAW, asks to format, or has read errors? Image it with ddrescue first, then recover files with TestDisk or PhotoRec on the copy.
corrupted.summary: Corruption often follows pulling the cable without ejecting, a power cut, or failing parts. The files may still be there. Do not run repair tools on the original first, because they can change data.
corrupted.riskNote: The drive may be weak, and repair tools like CHKDSK on the original can change data before you have a copy.
stopFirst: Do not run CHKDSK, fsck, or Disk Utility repair on the original before copying your data.
Do not click Format when the computer says the drive needs formatting.
Do not install recovery software onto the affected drive or save files back to it.

steps.title: Stop using the drive
steps.detail: Eject it safely if you can. Check whether it is making noises. If it clicks or grinds, read the clicking guide instead.

steps.title: Check its health
steps.detail: Use CrystalDiskInfo or smartmontools to read the SMART report. Some USB cases hide SMART, so a missing report does not mean it is fine.

steps.title: Try a different cable and port
steps.detail: A bad cable can mimic corruption. Plug directly into the computer, not through a hub, and keep the drive in its case, because many WD drives encrypt data through the case's board.

steps.title: Get a destination drive
steps.detail: You need a different drive at least as big as the damaged one for the image.

steps.title: Image with ddrescue
steps.detail: GNU ddrescue (or HDDSuperClone on Linux) copies the drive, skipping unreadable spots and returning to them later; keep its map file. Type the damaged drive first and the destination second; swapping them erases your data.

steps.title: Recover from the image
steps.detail: Run TestDisk on the image to rebuild partitions or list files, then PhotoRec if needed. Never work on the original.

corrupted.callPro: If imaging keeps stalling, the drive makes noises, or the data is critical, stop and talk to a professional.

faq.q: Should I run CHKDSK first?
faq.a: No. It can rewrite damaged data. Image the drive first and repair or recover from the copy.

faq.q: Why does it say the drive is RAW?
faq.a: The computer cannot read the file system, often because of an unsafe unplug or damage. TestDisk can often restore it.

faq.q: Why can't I see SMART data?
faq.a: Many USB enclosures do not pass it through. That is common and does not mean the drive is healthy.

encrypted.title: Recover Data From an Encrypted External Drive
encrypted.metaDescription: Locked out of an encrypted external drive such as WD My Passport, BitLocker or Mac encryption? Find your key first. Without it, recovery is unrealistic.
encrypted.summary: Many external drives encrypt data, either with software like BitLocker or Mac's built-in drive encryption, or with hardware encryption, as on many WD My Passport and My Book drives. Without the password or recovery key, recovery is not realistic.
encrypted.riskNote: Unlocking with a known key is low risk, but taking a hardware-encrypted drive out of its enclosure can make the data unreadable.
stopFirst: Do not remove the drive from its enclosure if it uses hardware encryption. The key may be tied to the bridge board, and a different adapter can show unreadable data.
Do not format or reset it. That destroys the key and the data.
Do not trust tools or people claiming to crack or brute-force strong encryption.

steps.title: Find out what kind of encryption it is
steps.detail: Look at the model and software. WD My Passport and My Book often use hardware encryption, even if you never set a password. Others use BitLocker To Go, Mac drive encryption or VeraCrypt.

steps.title: Find your recovery key
steps.detail: BitLocker keys are often saved in your Microsoft account (account.microsoft.com/devices/recoverykey), a work or school account, a printout or a file. A Mac-encrypted drive uses the password you set, which may be saved in the Mac's Keychain.

steps.title: Use the vendor's unlock tool
steps.detail: For password-protected WD drives, use the manufacturer's unlock software with your password while the drive stays in its original enclosure.

steps.title: Keep the original enclosure and cable
steps.detail: If the drive is hardware encrypted, keep it connected through the original bridge board. A spare adapter or direct SATA connection may show scrambled data.

steps.title: Copy data after unlocking
steps.detail: Once unlocked, copy your files to a different drive. If the drive is also faulty, image it with ddrescue while it is unlocked and still in its case. Type the drive first and the destination second; swapping them erases your data.

steps.title: Accept the limit if the key is lost
steps.detail: Without the password or recovery key, strong encryption cannot be broken in practice. Recovery tools will only find scrambled data.

encrypted.callPro: If the drive or its board is damaged and you hold the password or key, a professional may be able to help; without the key, no one can realistically recover the data.

faq.q: Why is my WD drive unreadable outside its case?
faq.a: Many WD My Passport and My Book drives encrypt data using a key tied to the bridge board. A different adapter can leave the data unreadable.

faq.q: Where is my BitLocker recovery key?
faq.a: Often in your Microsoft account online, a work or school account, a printed page or a saved file.

faq.q: Can someone crack it for me?
faq.a: Not realistically. Strong encryption is designed to resist this, so be wary of anyone who says otherwise.

deleted.title: Recover Deleted Files From an Internal Hard Drive
deleted.metaDescription: Deleted files on a hard drive are often still there until overwritten. Learn how to stop the damage and safely recover them with free tools like PhotoRec.
deleted.summary: When you delete a file, the computer usually just marks its space as free. The data stays on the disk until something new is written over it. The sooner you stop using the drive, the better your chances.
deleted.riskNote: If the drive is healthy, recovery only reads data, as long as you save results to a different drive.
stopFirst: Stop saving, downloading, installing or browsing on this drive right now. New data can overwrite your deleted files.
Do not install recovery software onto the affected drive. Install it on a different drive or run it from a USB stick.
Do not save recovered files back to the same drive. Always pick a different drive.

steps.title: Stop using the drive
steps.detail: If it is your Windows or Mac system drive, shut down now. Every minute the computer runs, it writes small files that can overwrite what you deleted.

steps.title: Check the Recycle Bin or Trash first
steps.detail: Open the Recycle Bin (Windows) or Trash (Mac). If your file is there, restore it and you are done. Also check cloud backups or File History and Time Machine.

steps.title: Prepare a second drive
steps.detail: Get a separate drive with enough free space to hold everything you want back. This is where recovered files will be saved.

steps.title: Run recovery from another computer or a USB stick
steps.detail: Best is to connect the drive to a second computer, or boot from a USB stick with TestDisk and PhotoRec. This keeps the original drive untouched.

steps.title: Try TestDisk first for whole folders
steps.detail: TestDisk can often list deleted files with their original names and folders. Copy what you need to your second drive.

steps.title: Use PhotoRec if names are lost
steps.detail: PhotoRec scans for file types such as photos and documents. It brings back the contents, but file names and folders are usually gone, so you sort them afterwards.

steps.title: Check your recovered files
steps.detail: Open a sample of files to be sure they work. Keep the original drive unchanged until you are happy with the results.

deleted.callPro: If the drive starts making odd noises, disappears, or the files are very valuable and recovery fails, stop and talk to a professional before trying more.

faq.q: Can I get back files I emptied from the Recycle Bin?
faq.a: Often yes, because emptying the bin only frees the space, so stop using the drive right away. Some newer SMR drives clear freed space like an SSD does, which lowers the odds.

faq.q: Why did my recovered files lose their names?
faq.a: PhotoRec finds files by their content, not by the file table, so names and folders are not saved. TestDisk can sometimes keep names if the file table is still intact.

faq.q: Is it a problem that I kept using the computer after deleting?
faq.a: It lowers the odds a bit, because new data may land on the freed space. Stop now and recover what is left.

formatted.title: Recover Files From a Formatted Hard Drive
formatted.metaDescription: Accidentally formatted a hard drive? Quick format is often recoverable, full format on Windows is not. Learn what to do and which free tools to use.
formatted.summary: A quick format wipes the drive's table of contents but leaves most of your data in place, so recovery is often possible. A full format on modern Windows (Vista and later) writes zeros over everything, and that data is gone for good.
formatted.riskNote: Software recovery only reads from the drive, but writing anything new to it can destroy what is left.
stopFirst: Do not copy, save or install anything onto the formatted drive. New data overwrites what you want back.
Do not format it again, and do not reinstall the operating system on it.
Do not install recovery software onto the formatted drive. Use a different drive.

steps.title: Work out which kind of format you did
steps.detail: A quick format finished in seconds or minutes. A full format ran for a long time. On Windows Vista and later, a full format writes zeros, so the old data cannot be brought back.

steps.title: Stop using the drive
steps.detail: If it was your system drive and you reinstalled the operating system, the new install has already overwritten some data. Stop and do not install anything else.

steps.title: Attach it to a second computer
steps.detail: Connect the drive as a secondary drive, or boot from a USB stick with recovery tools. Prepare a separate drive with enough space to save results.

steps.title: Try TestDisk to restore the old structure
steps.detail: TestDisk can search for the lost partition and may bring back folders with their original names. This works best after a quick format.

steps.title: Use PhotoRec if TestDisk finds nothing
steps.detail: PhotoRec scans the whole drive for known file types and saves them to your second drive. Names and folders are usually lost, but the content is back.

steps.title: Check what you got
steps.detail: Open a few files of each type. If many are damaged or missing, the drive may have been fully formatted or overwritten, or it may be a newer SMR drive that clears freed space.

formatted.callPro: If the drive is making noises, is not detected, or the data is critical and software scans fail, stop and consult a professional.

faq.q: Can I recover data after a full format?
faq.a: On Windows Vista and newer, a full format writes zeros over the disk, so the data is gone. A quick format is a very different story and is often recoverable.

faq.q: Did reinstalling Windows destroy my files?
faq.a: It overwrote part of the drive, so some files are lost. Others may still be there, so stop using it and scan it from another computer with PhotoRec.

faq.q: Will I get my folders and file names back?
faq.a: Sometimes with TestDisk. With PhotoRec, files usually come back with generic names and are sorted by type.

not-detected.title: Hard Drive Not Showing Up or Not Detected
not-detected.metaDescription: Hard drive not detected or not showing in Windows or Mac? Check cables, ports and Disk Management first, then recover data without more damage.
not-detected.summary: A drive that does not show up may have a loose cable, a bad port, a lost partition, or a real hardware fault. The first checks are simple and safe. If the drive is silent, clicking, or hot, the cause may be physical.
not-detected.riskNote: Cable and software checks are safe, but repeated power-ups of a physically failing drive can make the damage worse.
stopFirst: Do not keep powering the drive on and off to see if it comes back. Each attempt can add wear if it is failing.
Do not click Initialize or Format if your computer offers it. That can erase the data.
Do not open the drive. Hard drives need a cleanroom, and dust ruins them.

steps.title: Listen and feel
steps.detail: A healthy drive spins up with a soft hum. If you hear clicking, grinding or beeping, stop and read the clicking guide; if you smell burning, unplug it and read the won't-power-on guide.

steps.title: Check the BIOS or UEFI
steps.detail: Restart and open the BIOS screen. If the drive is listed with its correct model and size, the hardware is talking to the computer and the problem is likely software or partition related.

steps.title: Swap the cable and port
steps.detail: Try a different SATA data cable and a different port, and check the power connector. Bad cables cause many drive-not-found problems.

steps.title: Look in Disk Management or Disk Utility
steps.detail: On Windows, open Disk Management. On Mac, open Disk Utility. If the drive is listed but has no letter or says Raw or Unallocated, do not format it.

steps.title: Check drive health
steps.detail: Use CrystalDiskInfo on Windows or smartmontools on Linux or Mac to read the SMART health report. Warnings like Caution or Bad mean the drive is failing.

steps.title: Copy the data off or make an image
steps.detail: If the drive is readable but weak, image it with ddrescue onto another drive, then use TestDisk or PhotoRec on the image, not the original. Type the failing drive first and the destination second; swapping them erases your data.

steps.title: Stop if it still does not appear
steps.detail: If it is not seen in the BIOS after a cable swap, the drive or its circuit board has likely failed. Further DIY is risky.

not-detected.callPro: If the drive is missing from the BIOS after trying a new cable and port, or it makes any unusual noise, stop and consider a professional with a cleanroom.

faq.q: My drive shows up but says Raw or needs formatting. What now?
faq.a: Do not format it. The file table may be damaged, and TestDisk or PhotoRec can often still reach your files, ideally working on an image.

faq.q: Could it just be a cable?
faq.a: Yes, that is very common. Try another cable, port, and power connector before assuming the drive is dead.

faq.q: Can I fix it by swapping the circuit board?
faq.a: Not as a DIY fix. Each board has a ROM chip with data unique to that drive, which must be moved onto the new board, so leave it to specialists.

clicking.title: Hard Drive Clicking, Grinding or Beeping
clicking.metaDescription: A clicking, grinding or beeping hard drive is failing mechanically. Learn what not to do, why the freezer trick is a myth, and when DIY is reasonable.
clicking.summary: Clicking, grinding or beeping usually means the moving parts inside, such as the read/write heads, are damaged or stuck. Every extra power-up can scratch the disk surface and destroy more data.
clicking.riskNote: Mechanical faults can get worse every time the drive is powered on, and real repairs need a cleanroom.
stopFirst: Power it off and leave it off. Do not keep trying, because each power-up can scratch the platters.
Do not put the drive in the freezer, tap it, or shake it. The freezer trick is a myth that can cause condensation damage.
Never open the drive. Dust in a normal room ruins the platters.
Do not run recovery scans, CHKDSK or other repair tools on it. Heavy reading stresses a failing drive; imaging (below) is the only DIY step worth trying.

steps.title: Unplug it now
steps.detail: Shut down and disconnect the drive. Note what you heard (clicking, grinding, beeping, or not spinning) because it helps when talking to an expert.

steps.title: Decide how valuable the data is
steps.detail: If it is irreplaceable, the safest choice is a professional lab with a cleanroom. If it is replaceable or you accept the risk, read on.

steps.title: Check the noise source
steps.detail: Make sure the noise really came from the drive and not a fan. Do not keep testing cables and power on an internal drive, because clicking is rarely a cable problem.

steps.title: Try one careful attempt, if you accept the risk
steps.detail: Boot a second computer from a Linux live USB and connect the drive once. If it spins up and appears, start imaging right away with HDDSuperClone or ddrescue (both run on Linux) onto a different healthy drive.

steps.title: Image, don't copy
steps.detail: These tools read the easy areas first and skip bad spots, saving the most data before the drive gets worse. Type the failing drive first and the destination second; swapping them erases your data.

steps.title: Recover from the image
steps.detail: Once you have an image, run TestDisk or PhotoRec on the image file, never on the original failing drive.

steps.title: Stop at the first sign of trouble
steps.detail: If it clicks, stalls, or disappears again, power it off. Further attempts lower the odds for a professional.

clicking.callPro: If the data matters and the drive clicks, grinds, beeps or will not spin, stop and have a professional with a cleanroom look at it.

faq.q: Does the freezer trick work?
faq.a: No. It can cause condensation and make the damage worse. Experts and data recovery communities advise against it.

faq.q: Can I open the drive and fix it myself?
faq.a: No. Opening a hard drive outside a cleanroom lets in dust that can scratch the platters. Head replacement needs special tools and matching parts.

faq.q: Is it worth trying once myself?
faq.a: Only if the data is not critical. Keep it to one careful attempt, and image the drive immediately if it works.

no-power.title: Hard Drive Not Spinning or Won't Power On
no-power.metaDescription: Hard drive silent, not spinning, or smells burnt? Check power and cables safely, learn why not to retry again and again, and when to see a professional.
no-power.summary: If the drive makes no sound and does not spin, the cause may be a bad cable, bad power supply, or a failed circuit board or motor. A burnt smell suggests an electrical fault, which can be dangerous to keep trying.
no-power.riskNote: Simple cable and power checks are fine, but repeated attempts on a drive with a burnt board or stuck motor can cause more harm.
stopFirst: Unplug it right away if you smell burning or see scorch marks. Do not power it up again.
Do not power-cycle it again and again hoping it starts. Limit yourself to one or two careful tries.
Do not use the freezer trick, and never open the drive. It needs a cleanroom.
Do not swap circuit boards yourself. Each board has a ROM chip with drive-specific data that must be moved over, which is a job for a lab.

steps.title: Look and smell
steps.detail: Check the circuit board on the underside for burn marks, a burnt chip, or a burnt smell. If you see or smell any, leave it unplugged.

steps.title: Try one other power source
steps.detail: Use a different SATA power connector, or try the drive in a different computer. A weak power supply is a common cause.

steps.title: Use a good cable for that same try
steps.detail: Swap the data cable and port at the same time, so one attempt tests everything. In a desktop, check that other drives on the same power cable work.

steps.title: Listen for spin-up
steps.detail: During that try, rest your hand lightly on the drive. A faint hum or vibration means it spins. Silence means a power, board or motor issue.

steps.title: If it spins and shows up, image it
steps.detail: Use HDDSuperClone (Linux) or ddrescue to copy it to a different drive. Type the failing drive first and the destination second; swapping them erases your data.

steps.title: Recover from the image
steps.detail: Run TestDisk or PhotoRec on the image file, not the original.

steps.title: Stop if it stays dead
steps.detail: A drive that never spins needs hardware repair by a professional. More attempts will not help.

no-power.callPro: If it does not spin after trying another cable and power source, or there is a burnt smell or scorch marks, stop and use a professional.

faq.q: My drive is dead but not clicking. Is that better or worse?
faq.a: Neither is good. Silence points to power, circuit board or motor trouble. Check the cable and power first, then consider a professional.

faq.q: Can I replace the circuit board myself?
faq.a: Not as a DIY fix. The board's ROM chip holds unique data for that drive and must be moved to the new board, which experts do with special tools.

faq.q: Is a burnt smell always the end?
faq.a: Not always. Sometimes only the protection part on the board has blown and the data is fine, but it needs a careful repair by an expert.

liquid-fire.title: Water, Liquid or Fire Damaged Hard Drive
liquid-fire.metaDescription: Hard drive got wet, flooded or burned? Do not power it on, do not use rice or heat. Learn what to do next to give a professional the best chance.
liquid-fire.summary: Liquid can short the circuit board and corrode parts inside, and fire or heat can warp the drive. Powering it on can cause a short or scratch the platters, so the safest move is to keep it off and get professional help.
liquid-fire.riskNote: Power, heat, or opening the drive can turn recoverable damage into permanent loss.
stopFirst: Do not power it on. Not even once to see if it works.
Do not dry it with a hair dryer, oven or heater, and do not bury it in rice. Heat can warp parts, and rice adds dust and starch without drying the inside.
Do not open the drive or try to clean the platters.
Do not shake it or rinse it to remove dirt or salt water.

steps.title: Keep it unpowered
steps.detail: Unplug it and leave it off; powering a wet drive can short the board or scratch the disk. If it is inside a wet or burned laptop, unplug the charger and stay away from a swollen, hot or smoking battery, which can catch fire.

steps.title: Note what happened
steps.detail: Was it clean water, salt water, a sugary drink, flood mud, smoke or flames? This matters, because salt and mud corrode quickly.

steps.title: Keep it damp if it came from a flood
steps.detail: If it is muddy or salty, sealing it in a plastic bag without drying it can slow corrosion until an expert sees it. Do not let it dry out in the open.

steps.title: Pack it gently
steps.detail: Wrap it in a soft cloth, put it in a box with padding, and avoid bumps or heat.

steps.title: Contact a professional soon
steps.detail: Corrosion keeps spreading with time, so do not wait. Choose a lab that works in a cleanroom and ask about their policy before you pay.

liquid-fire.callPro: Water, liquid, smoke or fire damage should go to a professional with a cleanroom before anyone powers the drive on.

faq.q: Will putting it in rice help?
faq.a: No. Rice does not pull water out of a drive, and it can add dust and starch. Keep it off and get professional help.

faq.q: Can I dry it with a hair dryer?
faq.a: No. Heat can warp parts and drive moisture further inside. Leave drying and cleaning to an expert.

faq.q: What if it was fully dry and looks fine?
faq.a: Looking fine is not proof it is safe, because residue can short the board. Powering it is a gamble, so a professional is safer for important data.

corrupted.title: Fix a Corrupted or Unreadable Hard Drive
corrupted.metaDescription: Hard drive corrupted, shows RAW, asks to format, or has read errors? Image it with ddrescue first, then recover files with TestDisk or PhotoRec safely.
corrupted.summary: Corruption means the drive's file records are damaged, often after a power loss, a bad shutdown, or failing sectors. The files may still be there. Do not run repair tools on the original first, because they can change data.
corrupted.riskNote: The drive may be weakening, and repair tools like CHKDSK on the original can change data before you have a copy.
stopFirst: Do not run CHKDSK, fsck, or Disk Utility repair on the original before copying your data. Repairs can rewrite data.
Do not click Format when Windows says the drive needs to be formatted.
Do not install recovery software onto the affected drive, and do not save recovered files back to it.

steps.title: Stop using the drive
steps.detail: Shut down or unmount it. If it is making noises, read the clicking guide instead.

steps.title: Check its health
steps.detail: Use CrystalDiskInfo (Windows) or smartmontools to read the SMART report. Reallocated, pending or uncorrectable sectors mean the disk is wearing out.

steps.title: Get a second drive that is as large
steps.detail: You need a different drive at least as big as the damaged one to hold an image of it.

steps.title: Image the drive with ddrescue
steps.detail: GNU ddrescue (or HDDSuperClone on Linux) copies the drive, skipping unreadable spots and returning to them later; keep its map file so you can resume. Type the damaged drive first and the destination second; swapping them erases your data.

steps.title: Work on the image, not the original
steps.detail: Make a copy of the image if you can. Then run TestDisk to rebuild partitions or restore folders, on the image only.

steps.title: Use PhotoRec as a fallback
steps.detail: If the folder structure is too damaged, PhotoRec carves out files by type from the image. Names will be generic.

steps.title: Store the recovered files safely
steps.detail: Save to a third location if you can, and check that the files open correctly.

corrupted.callPro: If imaging keeps stalling, the drive makes noises, or the data is critical, stop and talk to a professional rather than hammering the drive.

faq.q: Should I run CHKDSK to fix it?
faq.a: Not first. It can rewrite damaged data. Make an image of the drive, then repair or recover from that copy.

faq.q: What is a disk image?
faq.a: It is an exact copy of everything on the drive saved as a file or onto another drive. It lets you try recovery over and over without risking the original.

faq.q: Why does it say the drive is RAW?
faq.a: The computer cannot read the file system, usually due to damage. The data is often still there and TestDisk may restore it.

encrypted.title: Recover Data From an Encrypted Hard Drive
encrypted.metaDescription: Locked out of a BitLocker, FileVault or other encrypted hard drive? Find your recovery key first. Without the key or password, recovery is not realistic.
encrypted.summary: Encryption scrambles your data so that only the right password or recovery key can unlock it. If the drive is healthy and you have the key, getting files back is usually simple. Without it, recovery is not realistic, and anyone promising otherwise should not be trusted.
encrypted.riskNote: Unlocking with a known key is low risk, but guessing or tampering with a failing encrypted drive can lock you out for good.
stopFirst: Do not format, reset, or reinstall the operating system. That destroys the encryption headers and your chance of unlocking.
Do not keep guessing passwords on a drive that locks you out after failed tries.
Do not trust tools or sites that claim to crack or brute-force strong encryption.

steps.title: Work out which encryption it is
steps.detail: On Windows it is often BitLocker, and on a Mac it is FileVault. Others include VeraCrypt, or LUKS on Linux. Each has its own unlock method.

steps.title: Find your recovery key
steps.detail: BitLocker keys are often saved to your Microsoft account (account.microsoft.com/devices/recoverykey), a work or school account, a printout, or a USB stick. FileVault can use your Apple Account or a recovery key you saved.

steps.title: Check old notes and password managers
steps.detail: Search email, password managers, printed pages, and cloud storage for a long number or phrase. A recovery key is usually a 48-digit number for BitLocker.

steps.title: Unlock a healthy drive and copy the files
steps.detail: Use the key to unlock the drive in the normal system, then copy your files to a different drive.

steps.title: If the drive is also failing, image it first
steps.detail: Only worth it if you have the key. Use ddrescue to copy the encrypted drive to another drive and unlock the copy later. Type the failing drive first and the destination second; swapping them erases your data.

steps.title: Accept the limit if no key exists
steps.detail: Without the password or recovery key, modern encryption cannot be reasonably broken. Recovery tools like PhotoRec will only return scrambled data.

encrypted.callPro: If you hold the key but the drive is also failing or damaged, a professional can image it for you; without the key, no one can realistically recover the data.

faq.q: Where is my BitLocker recovery key?
faq.a: Often in your Microsoft account online, or in a work or school account, a printed page, or a saved file or USB stick.

faq.q: Can someone crack the encryption for me?
faq.a: Not realistically. Modern encryption with a strong password is built to resist this, so be careful of anyone who says otherwise.

faq.q: What if I forgot my FileVault password?
faq.a: Try your Apple Account reset or the recovery key you saved when you turned it on. Without those, the data cannot be unlocked.

deleted.title: Recover Deleted Photos from an SD or microSD Card
deleted.metaDescription: Deleted photos or videos from an SD or microSD card can often be recovered with PhotoRec. Stop shooting, then follow this safe step-by-step guide.
deleted.summary: When you delete files from an SD card, the data usually stays until new photos or videos overwrite it. SD cards do not use TRIM in most cameras and readers, so recovery odds are often good. The most important step is to stop using the card.
deleted.riskNote: Scanning a copy is safe, but taking even a few more photos can overwrite what you want back.
stopFirst: Stop taking photos or videos with the card right now.
Do not install recovery software onto the card.
Do not format the card, even if the camera or phone asks you to.

steps.title: Remove the card
steps.detail: Turn off the camera or phone and take the card out. Even just leaving it in can sometimes write small files.

steps.title: Check backups
steps.detail: Look for cloud backups, a second memory card slot, or copies on your phone or computer.

steps.title: Use a card reader
steps.detail: Plug the card into a computer with a USB card reader. On a full-size SD card or adapter, slide the lock switch down to Lock so the computer treats it as read-only, though some readers ignore it.

steps.title: Image the card
steps.detail: Use ddrescue to copy the whole card to an image file on your computer, then work from the image. Type the card first and the image file second; swapping them erases the card.

steps.title: Try TestDisk
steps.detail: Run TestDisk on the image to look for deleted files with their names. This is quick and worth trying.

steps.title: Run PhotoRec
steps.detail: PhotoRec can recover photos and videos, including many camera RAW formats, even if the file list is gone.

steps.title: Save somewhere else
steps.detail: Pick a folder on your computer or another drive as the destination. Never save back onto the card.

deleted.callPro: If the card is unstable, disconnects during copying, or the photos are irreplaceable and scans find nothing, stop and consult a professional.

faq.q: Can I recover photos I deleted from a camera card?
faq.a: Often yes, if you stopped using the card. Photos are usually still on it until new ones overwrite them.

faq.q: Does taking more photos hurt my chances?
faq.a: Yes. New pictures can be written over the deleted ones, so stop using the card immediately.

formatted.title: Recover Photos from a Formatted SD or microSD Card
formatted.metaDescription: Formatted an SD or microSD card by mistake? A quick format usually leaves photos recoverable. Image first, then use TestDisk and PhotoRec.
formatted.summary: Formatting in most cameras clears the file list but leaves most photos on the card. Formatting in a phone, a full format in Windows, or a camera's 'low-level' or 'secure' format often erases the data and lowers the odds.
formatted.riskNote: Recovery scans are safe on a copy, but taking new photos or formatting again overwrites the old data.
stopFirst: Do not take any more photos or videos with the card.
Do not format it again or choose a 'secure' or 'full' format.
Do not install recovery software onto the card.

steps.title: Remove the card
steps.detail: Switch off the device and take the card out so nothing new is written.

steps.title: Connect with a card reader
steps.detail: Use a USB card reader on a computer. On a full-size SD card or adapter, slide the lock switch down to Lock so the computer treats it as read-only, though some readers ignore it.

steps.title: Image the card
steps.detail: Use ddrescue to copy the entire card to a file on another disk, then do all later work on the copy. Type the card first and the image file second; swapping them erases the card.

steps.title: Look for the old layout
steps.detail: Run TestDisk on the image and use Analyse. It may find the old partition and let you copy files with names.

steps.title: Scan with PhotoRec
steps.detail: If TestDisk cannot, PhotoRec pulls out photos, videos and documents by their contents.

steps.title: Save to another drive
steps.detail: Recover to a folder on your computer, then open sample files to confirm they are intact.

formatted.callPro: If the card was fully formatted, reused heavily after formatting, or the images fail to copy, a professional may help, but chances are lower.

faq.q: Do formatted SD cards keep my photos?
faq.a: Usually a quick format does. Most photos remain until new ones are written, so recovery is often possible.

faq.q: Should I format the card again to fix it?
faq.a: Not until your files are safely recovered. Another format can overwrite more data.

not-detected.title: SD or microSD Card Not Detected or Not Reading
not-detected.metaDescription: SD or microSD card not showing up? Try a different reader, check the lock switch, and learn when a dead card needs professional chip-level help.
not-detected.summary: A card may not show up because of a dirty or bad reader, a missing drive letter, damaged file information, or a failed controller. Many cases are fixed by changing the reader. If the card is truly dead, only a specialist can try chip-level recovery.
not-detected.riskNote: Simple checks are safe, but accepting a format prompt or forcing a damaged card can destroy what is left.
stopFirst: Do not click Format when the computer or camera asks.
Do not bend, force or clean the card contacts with anything abrasive.
Do not keep inserting and removing it many times.

steps.title: Try another reader
steps.detail: Use a different USB card reader and port, ideally on another computer. Many 'dead' cards are really bad readers.

steps.title: Look in Disk Management
steps.detail: On Windows use Disk Management, on Mac use Disk Utility. A card with no drive letter or showing RAW may still hold your data.

steps.title: Clean gently
steps.detail: Wipe the gold contacts with a dry, soft lint-free cloth. Do not use liquid.

steps.title: Image if it responds
steps.detail: If the card shows up at all, copy it right away with ddrescue, because failing cards often get worse. Type the card first and the destination second; swapping them erases the card.

steps.title: Recover from the image
steps.detail: Run TestDisk and PhotoRec on the copy, saving to another drive.

not-detected.callPro: If no reader detects the card, or it reports a tiny size such as 0 MB, the controller or memory has likely failed and needs a lab with flash recovery tools, since most microSD cards are sealed monolith chips.

faq.q: Why does my microSD card show nothing in the reader?
faq.a: The reader, adapter or card contacts may be bad, or the card's controller may have failed. Try a different reader first.

faq.q: Can a dead SD card be recovered?
faq.a: Sometimes, by labs that read the memory directly, often by soldering to tiny test points on monolith cards. It is costly and not guaranteed.

no-power.title: SD or microSD Card Dead and Not Responding
no-power.metaDescription: SD or microSD card completely dead? Rule out the reader and adapter, then learn why a failed controller needs a lab with special flash recovery tools.
no-power.summary: A card cannot show a light or sound, so a dead card just does not respond anywhere. Check the reader, adapter and contacts first. If it is still dead, the controller is likely broken and the data can only be read with special equipment.
no-power.riskNote: A cracked or shorted card can be damaged further by repeated tries, and DIY opening or soldering destroys it.
stopFirst: Do not keep trying if the card feels hot or looks cracked.
Do not open the card or try to solder it.
Do not format it if it briefly appears and asks.

steps.title: Swap the reader and adapter
steps.detail: For a microSD card, test a different adapter as well as a different reader. Test the reader with another card to be sure.

steps.title: Check the card visually
steps.detail: Look for cracks, bent plastic, burn marks or missing contacts. If damaged, stop here.

steps.title: Try a second computer
steps.detail: Use a different computer and operating system if you can.

steps.title: Image if it responds
steps.detail: If the card appears even once, immediately copy it with ddrescue to another disk. Type the card first and the destination second; swapping them erases the card.

steps.title: Recover from the copy
steps.detail: Use TestDisk and PhotoRec on the image.

no-power.callPro: If the card is dead in every reader, a controller or monolith chip failure usually needs a lab with special flash recovery tools.

faq.q: Is a dead microSD card always lost?
faq.a: No, but DIY options are limited. If the memory chip is intact, a lab with special tools may read it.

faq.q: Could it just be my card reader?
faq.a: Yes, that is common. Try a different reader and adapter before giving up.

liquid-fire.title: SD or microSD Card Damaged by Water or Heat
liquid-fire.metaDescription: SD or microSD card went through the wash or got hot? Do not plug it in or heat-dry it. Learn the safest steps and when to call a professional.
liquid-fire.summary: Many SD cards are rated water resistant, and some survive being washed. Liquid, heat or fire can still corrode the contacts or damage the chip. Plugging in a wet or dirty card can short it.
liquid-fire.riskNote: Powering a wet or contaminated card can short it, and heat can permanently damage the memory chip.
stopFirst: Do not put the card in a camera, phone or reader while it is wet.
Do not use a hair dryer, oven, microwave or rice to dry it.
Do not scrub the contacts or take the card apart.

steps.title: Keep it out of devices
steps.detail: Do not test it in any device until it is fully dry and you have inspected it.

steps.title: Do not rinse or clean it
steps.detail: If it got salt water, mud or soda on it, leave it as it is. Cleaning off residue safely takes lab tools, so a professional should do it.

steps.title: Air dry only after clean water
steps.detail: If it only got fresh water, let it dry for several days at room temperature on a clean towel, with no heat. After salt water, soda, mud or fire, skip this and go to a professional.

steps.title: Inspect it
steps.detail: Look for corrosion, residue, cracks and warping. If you see any, do not insert it.

steps.title: Image it first
steps.detail: If it looks clean and shows up in a reader, copy it at once with ddrescue to another disk. Type the card first and the destination second; swapping them erases the card.

steps.title: Recover from the image
steps.detail: Use TestDisk and PhotoRec on the copy.

liquid-fire.callPro: If the card is burned, corroded, bent or still not detected after drying, stop and contact a professional rather than trying again.

faq.q: Can an SD card survive the washing machine?
faq.a: Often yes, if fully dried before use. Waiting several days is safer than rushing.

faq.q: Is it safe to dry a card with heat?
faq.a: No. Heat can damage the memory chip and its connections.

corrupted.title: Fix a Corrupted SD or microSD Card Without Losing Photos
corrupted.metaDescription: SD card says unreadable, RAW or asks to format? Image it first, then use TestDisk and PhotoRec. Skip format and chkdsk until your files are safe.
corrupted.summary: A card can become corrupted when removed during a write, when power dies, or when it wears out. The photos are often still there even if the camera shows an error. Making a copy before any repair keeps your options open.
corrupted.riskNote: Formatting, chkdsk or the camera's 'repair' prompts can overwrite the information needed to get your files back.
stopFirst: Do not click Format when the camera or computer asks to.
Do not run chkdsk or any 'repair' prompt before making an image.
Do not take more photos with the card.

steps.title: Stop and remove the card
steps.detail: Turn off the camera and take the card out. Avoid any prompt to fix or format it.

steps.title: Use a card reader
steps.detail: Put the card in a USB reader. On a full-size SD card or adapter, slide the lock switch down to Lock so the computer treats it as read-only, though some readers ignore it.

steps.title: Image the card
steps.detail: Use ddrescue to copy the card to an image file on another disk; it handles bad spots without stopping. Type the card first and the image file second; swapping them erases the card.

steps.title: Try TestDisk
steps.detail: Run TestDisk on the image to repair the partition or boot sector, or to browse the files.

steps.title: Use PhotoRec
steps.detail: If folders are lost, PhotoRec recovers photos and videos by type from the image.

steps.title: Save to a different drive
steps.detail: Recover only to your computer or another disk, never the card.

steps.title: Check the card for fakes
steps.detail: Once recovered, test the card with f3 or h2testw. These write test data, so only run them after your files are safe. A fake-capacity card often gets corrupted.

corrupted.callPro: If the card disconnects often, reports the wrong size, or imaging fails, stop and ask a professional.

faq.q: Why does my camera say the card needs formatting?
faq.a: The file system is damaged or unreadable. Your photos may still be on the card, so do not format yet.

faq.q: Could my SD card be counterfeit?
faq.a: It might be, especially if the price was too good. Fake cards claim more space than they have, so test with f3 or h2testw after recovery.

encrypted.title: Recover Data from an Encrypted SD or microSD Card
encrypted.metaDescription: Encrypted SD or microSD card from a phone or VeraCrypt? Without the key recovery is not realistic. Learn where keys and backups are often kept.
encrypted.summary: Some phones, cameras and apps encrypt memory cards, tying them to a device, a password or a key. If you do not have the key, recovery is not realistically possible. If you do, the data can usually be unlocked on the right device.
encrypted.riskNote: Resetting the phone, formatting the card or tapping 'Forget' on it in Android settings can delete the key and make the data unreadable for good.
stopFirst: Do not format the card or reset the phone or camera it was used in.
Do not use tools that claim to crack or guess passwords.
Do not install recovery software onto the card.

steps.title: Identify the encryption
steps.detail: Find out if it was locked by a phone's card encryption, a VeraCrypt volume, BitLocker To Go, or a camera or vendor app.

steps.title: Keep the original device
steps.detail: Some Android phones tie the key to the phone. Keep the phone and its lock-screen PIN or password.

steps.title: Find the password or key
steps.detail: Search your password manager, notes and emails. For BitLocker, check your Microsoft account for a recovery key.

steps.title: Unlock with the right tool
steps.detail: Use the same app or system that encrypted it, then copy files to another drive.

steps.title: Image if the card is damaged
steps.detail: Only useful if you can still unlock it, with the key or the original phone. Use ddrescue to copy the card first. Type the card first and the destination second; swapping them erases the card.

steps.title: Recover after unlocking
steps.detail: Use TestDisk or PhotoRec on the unlocked volume if files are missing.

encrypted.callPro: If the card is both encrypted and damaged, or you lost the key, a professional can only say whether anything is possible, and often it is not.

faq.q: Can I read an encrypted SD card without the key?
faq.a: Realistically no. Modern encryption with a strong password cannot be guessed or bypassed, so be wary of anyone who says otherwise.

faq.q: Will a new phone read my encrypted card?
faq.a: Often not, if the key was tied to the old phone. Keep the old device until you have copied your files.

deleted.title: Recover Deleted Files from an SSD
deleted.metaDescription: Deleted files on an internal SSD are usually gone for good because of TRIM. Learn what to do right now and what small chance remains.
deleted.summary: Modern SSDs use a feature called TRIM: the computer tells the drive which space is free, and the drive treats it as blank, usually right away, then erases it in the background. That means files deleted from an internal SSD are often gone within seconds to hours. Recovery mainly works when TRIM did not run, which is uncommon on Windows and Mac internal drives.
deleted.riskNote: Scanning is safe if you save results elsewhere, but while the SSD keeps running, the system can write new files or send more TRIM commands that erase what is left.
stopFirst: Shut the computer down now. Do not keep browsing or saving files on the SSD.
Do not install recovery software onto the SSD you are trying to recover from.
Do not run a disk cleanup, optimizer or 'trim' tool.

steps.title: Power off right away
steps.detail: The sooner the SSD stops running, the less time it has to erase deleted data in the background. If it is your only drive, shut down instead of just logging out.

steps.title: Check easy backups first
steps.detail: Look in the Recycle Bin or Trash, File History, Time Machine, OneDrive, iCloud or Google Drive. These work far better than recovery software on an SSD.

steps.title: Use a different computer
steps.detail: Connect the SSD to another computer with a USB adapter or dock, or boot from a USB stick with Linux. Do not boot from the SSD itself.

steps.title: Make an image if you can
steps.detail: An image is a full copy of the drive saved to another disk. Use ddrescue to copy the SSD to a drive at least as large, then work only on the copy. Type the SSD first and the destination second; swapping them erases your data.

steps.title: Scan the image with PhotoRec
steps.detail: PhotoRec searches for file contents instead of file names. Save everything it finds to a different drive than the one you are scanning.

steps.title: Try TestDisk for recent deletions
steps.detail: TestDisk can sometimes list deleted files with their original names. It is worth a try, but expect many results to be empty or damaged.

steps.title: Check what you got back
steps.detail: Open a sample of the recovered files. Files that open but are all zeros or blank mean the data was already erased.

deleted.callPro: If the files are extremely valuable, stop after powering off and ask a reputable professional whether anything is still recoverable, since DIY scanning cannot undo TRIM.

faq.q: What is TRIM and why does it matter?
faq.a: TRIM is a message from your operating system telling the SSD which blocks are free. The SSD then erases them, so deleted files really disappear.

faq.q: Are deleted files ever recoverable from an SSD?
faq.a: Sometimes. Results vary with the drive, operating system and settings, and external USB SSDs or older setups may not run TRIM. Treat it as a long shot.

faq.q: Does recovery software work better on an SSD than a hard drive?
faq.a: No, usually worse. A hard drive keeps deleted data until it is overwritten, but an SSD often wipes it on purpose.

formatted.title: Recover Data from a Formatted SSD
formatted.metaDescription: A formatted SSD often loses its data to TRIM within moments. Learn what to do first and when recovery with TestDisk or PhotoRec has a chance.
formatted.summary: Formatting an SSD, especially a full format or a reinstall of the operating system, commonly triggers TRIM, which erases the old data. Quick formats on internal SSDs are usually not recoverable. External or older setups that skip TRIM may still hold data.
formatted.riskNote: Reinstalling Windows or writing new files on the SSD speeds up permanent loss, so careless steps can end any chance of recovery.
stopFirst: Do not copy new files to the SSD or reinstall the operating system on it.
Do not install recovery software on the formatted SSD.
Do not format it again, even if a prompt suggests it.

steps.title: Power down
steps.detail: Turn the computer off. SSDs keep cleaning up in the background while they are powered, which can erase what is left.

steps.title: Move the SSD to another computer
steps.detail: Use a USB adapter or dock, or boot the same computer from a USB Linux stick. Never boot from the formatted SSD.

steps.title: Check for a full or quick format
steps.detail: Think back to what happened. A quick format only clears the index, but on an SSD the data may still be trimmed. A reinstall or full format is almost always final.

steps.title: Image the SSD
steps.detail: Use ddrescue to copy the whole drive to a disk at least as large, then try recovery on the copy as many times as you need. Type the SSD first and the destination second; swapping them erases your data.

steps.title: Look for the lost partition
steps.detail: Run TestDisk on the image. If the old partition is found, you may be able to browse and copy the files.

steps.title: Scan by file type
steps.detail: If TestDisk finds nothing, run PhotoRec on the image. It will recover whatever file contents still exist, without folder names.

steps.title: Save results elsewhere
steps.detail: Write recovered files to a separate drive and open some to confirm they work.

formatted.callPro: If the data is irreplaceable and TestDisk and PhotoRec find nothing, a professional is your only remaining option, though success on a trimmed SSD is unlikely.

faq.q: Will a quick format on an SSD wipe my files?
faq.a: Often yes. The format itself keeps data, but TRIM usually follows and erases it. Odds are better on external SSDs or older systems without TRIM.

faq.q: Can a professional get trimmed data back?
faq.a: Usually not. Once TRIM has run, the SSD reports that space as blank, and a lab mostly helps when the SSD itself has failed.

not-detected.title: SSD Not Detected or Not Showing Up
not-detected.metaDescription: An SSD that does not appear or shows a wrong name and size may have failed firmware. Learn safe checks and when to stop and call a professional.
not-detected.summary: If your computer cannot see the SSD, the cause could be a loose cable, a bad port, or a failed controller. A drive that appears with a strange name or tiny size, such as 'SATAFIRM S11', has a firmware or controller failure and is not a home repair.
not-detected.riskNote: Simple cable and port checks are safe, but repeated power cycling or firmware tools can permanently damage a failing controller.
stopFirst: Do not run firmware flashing tools or 'repair' utilities you found online.
Do not keep power cycling the drive hoping it comes back.
Do not open the drive or use heat or cold on it.

steps.title: Check the basics
steps.detail: With the computer off and unplugged, reseat the SATA or M.2 connection, then try another cable, port or enclosure. Test with a second computer if possible.

steps.title: Look in BIOS and Disk Management
steps.detail: See if the SSD appears in the BIOS or UEFI setup. In Windows, check Disk Management or Disk Utility on a Mac. It might be present but missing a drive letter.

steps.title: Read the name and size
steps.detail: If the drive shows as an odd name like SATAFIRM S11, or as a few megabytes, the controller or firmware has failed. Stop here.

steps.title: Check its health
steps.detail: If it does appear, use smartmontools or CrystalDiskInfo to view health data. Warnings such as low spare blocks or media errors mean the drive is failing.

steps.title: Image immediately if it works
steps.detail: A drive that appears only some of the time may stop for good. Copy it right away with ddrescue to another disk. Type the SSD first and the destination second; swapping them erases your data.

steps.title: Recover from the image
steps.detail: Use TestDisk to find lost partitions on the image, then PhotoRec for file contents if needed.

not-detected.callPro: If the SSD never appears or shows the wrong name or size, stop and consult a professional, because many SSDs encrypt data inside the controller and only a specialist can work around a dead one.

faq.q: Why does my SSD show up as SATAFIRM S11?
faq.a: That is a known failure mode where the controller cannot load its firmware and uses a basic safe mode name. Your data is not accessible with normal tools.

faq.q: Can I swap the circuit board to fix an SSD?
faq.a: No, because SSD controllers are tied to the data, often with built-in encryption. Even on hard drives a board swap needs the ROM chip moved, which is lab work.

no-power.title: SSD Dead or Won't Power On
no-power.metaDescription: A dead SSD with no activity or detection usually has a power or controller fault. See what safe checks to try before involving a professional.
no-power.summary: A dead SSD may be fine and the problem lies in the cable, port, adapter or power supply. If those check out, the controller or a power component on the SSD may have failed. SSDs have no moving parts, so there is nothing to listen for.
no-power.riskNote: Checking cables is safe, but repeatedly applying power to a drive with a short circuit can damage it more.
stopFirst: Do not keep plugging it in if you smell burning or see scorch marks.
Do not try to repair the circuit board yourself.
Do not keep power cycling it again and again hoping it comes back.

steps.title: Check for physical damage
steps.detail: Look for burn marks, a cracked board or bent connector pins. If you see damage, stop.

steps.title: Rule out the computer
steps.detail: Try a different cable, port, adapter or computer. Many 'dead' SSDs are really bad USB enclosures or cables.

steps.title: Test in another way
steps.detail: For M.2 drives, try a different slot or a USB-NVMe enclosure. For SATA, try another power cable.

steps.title: Wait before retrying
steps.detail: Some drives need a few minutes on power to recover after a sudden power loss. Do this once: leave it powered in a BIOS screen, not a running operating system, for about 10 minutes, and unplug it if it gets hot.

steps.title: Image if it responds
steps.detail: If the drive reappears, copy it with ddrescue to another disk before doing anything else. Type the SSD first and the destination second; swapping them erases your data.

steps.title: Recover from the copy
steps.detail: Run TestDisk or PhotoRec on the image, saving results to a different drive.

no-power.callPro: If the SSD is still not detected on a known-good cable and computer, the controller has likely failed and only a professional can attempt recovery.

faq.q: How can I tell if my SSD is dead or just the cable?
faq.a: Test it on a different cable, port and computer. If it fails everywhere, the drive itself is the problem.

faq.q: Does a dead SSD mean my data is gone?
faq.a: Not necessarily, but because many SSDs encrypt data and tie it to the controller, recovery is harder than with hard drives.

liquid-fire.title: SSD Damaged by Water, Fire or Impact
liquid-fire.metaDescription: Water, fire or heat damage to an SSD needs careful handling. Learn what not to do, including never powering it on, and when to call a professional.
liquid-fire.summary: Liquid, smoke, heat or a hard impact can short out an SSD or crack its memory chips. Powering it on can finish the damage. Your best chance is to keep it off and let a specialist look at it.
liquid-fire.riskNote: Powering on or heat-drying a damaged SSD can short the board and destroy data that was otherwise intact.
stopFirst: Do not plug the SSD in or power on the device it is in.
Do not dry it with a hair dryer, oven, rice or any heat.
Do not shake it, clean the contacts or open it.

steps.title: Disconnect power
steps.detail: If the SSD is in a laptop, unplug the charger, and remove the battery and SSD only if they come out easily. If the battery is swollen, hot or smoking, do not handle it; move away and call the fire service.

steps.title: Keep it still and dry
steps.detail: Place the drive in a clean, dry, anti-static bag or container. Do not rinse or wipe it, whatever the liquid was.

steps.title: Note what happened
steps.detail: Write down the kind of liquid or the heat exposure. This helps any specialist decide on the safest approach.

steps.title: Check for backups
steps.detail: While you wait, look for cloud backups, other copies and old backup drives. These may save the day.

steps.title: Decide on professional help
steps.detail: The only safe options are to leave it alone or send it to a lab that handles liquid damage. Ask about their no-fix, no-fee policy first.

liquid-fire.callPro: Contact a professional before attempting any power-on, since damaged SSDs are very fragile and DIY steps usually reduce the chance of recovery.

faq.q: Can I dry out a wet SSD and try it?
faq.a: No. Even after it looks dry, residue on the board can cause shorts. Do not use heat or rice.

faq.q: Is a burned SSD always unrecoverable?
faq.a: Not always. If the memory chips are intact, a specialist may be able to repair the board so the original controller can read them, but results vary a lot.

corrupted.title: Fix a Corrupted or RAW SSD Safely
corrupted.metaDescription: SSD shows RAW, asks to format, or has unreadable files? Make an image first, then use TestDisk and PhotoRec. Do not format or run chkdsk yet.
corrupted.summary: Corruption means the drive's file index or partition information is damaged, even though the data may still be there. Sometimes it is a software issue, and sometimes the SSD is starting to fail. Work from a copy to avoid making it worse.
corrupted.riskNote: Letting Windows format or repair the drive, or running chkdsk, can overwrite the index information you need to recover your files.
stopFirst: Do not click Format when the system says the drive must be formatted.
Do not run chkdsk or any 'repair' prompt before making a copy.
Do not install recovery software onto the problem SSD.

steps.title: Stop and check health
steps.detail: Use smartmontools or CrystalDiskInfo to look at the drive's health. Many errors or low remaining life suggest the SSD is failing.

steps.title: Back up what is readable
steps.detail: If you can open the drive, copy important files to another disk right now.

steps.title: Image the drive
steps.detail: Use ddrescue to copy the SSD to a drive at least as large, and keep its map file so the copy can resume if the SSD disconnects. Type the SSD first and the destination second; swapping them erases your data.

steps.title: Look for the partition
steps.detail: Open the image in TestDisk and run an Analyse. It can often find and restore a lost partition or repair the boot sector.

steps.title: Copy files out
steps.detail: If TestDisk shows your folders, copy the files to a different drive. Do not write the repair back to the original yet.

steps.title: Use PhotoRec as a backup plan
steps.detail: If the folders cannot be found, PhotoRec can pull files by type from the image, though names will be lost.

steps.title: Repair only at the end
steps.detail: After everything is safely copied, you can reformat the SSD or run Windows repair tools. If the health check showed errors, replace the SSD instead of trusting it again.

corrupted.callPro: If the SSD disconnects repeatedly, reports very few usable blocks, or the imaging stalls, stop and get professional help.

faq.q: Why does my SSD say it needs to be formatted?
faq.a: The file system information is damaged or unreadable. Your files may still exist, so do not format.

faq.q: Is it safe to run chkdsk on an SSD?
faq.a: Not before you have a copy. Chkdsk changes the drive and can delete data it cannot fix.

encrypted.title: Recover Data from an Encrypted SSD
encrypted.metaDescription: Encrypted SSDs need the password or recovery key. Find BitLocker, FileVault or VeraCrypt keys and learn why brute force is not a real option.
encrypted.summary: If your SSD is protected with BitLocker, FileVault, VeraCrypt or built-in hardware encryption, the data is scrambled without the key. Without the password or recovery key, recovery is not realistically possible. The good news is that keys are often stored somewhere you can find.
encrypted.riskNote: Wrong attempts, resets, or erasing the drive's encryption can make the data permanently unreadable.
stopFirst: Do not reset, secure erase or 'crypto erase' the SSD.
Do not reinstall the operating system over the encrypted drive.
Do not trust any site or service that promises to crack encryption.

steps.title: Identify the encryption type
steps.detail: Look for BitLocker on Windows, FileVault on Mac, VeraCrypt volumes, or a hardware password set in the BIOS or drive utility.

steps.title: Find the recovery key
steps.detail: For BitLocker, sign in at your Microsoft account's recovery key page or check work or school accounts, printouts and USB keys. For FileVault, check iCloud or the key you saved; on newer Macs the SSD is built in and can only be unlocked in that Mac.
